patient.chief_complaint: Five-day progressive ascending limb weakness with global areflexia and new unilateral ptosis — no ophthalmoplegia, no diplopia.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. C. is a 57-year-old financial analyst presenting with a 5-day history of progressive bilateral limb weakness and numbness. On day 1 he noted bilateral limb numbness. By day 2 he had bilateral toe weakness. By day 5, weakness had progressed to involve both proximal and distal muscles of all extremities. He can no longer walk independently. He notices a new partial drooping of his left eyelid — this is an isolated unilateral ptosis without any diplopia and with full extraocular movements in all directions. He denies any recent respiratory illness, diarrheal illness, or viral syndrome. He has no dysphagia or dysarthria. He has no diurnal variation in his ptosis — it is present consistently throughout the day, does not worsen with fatigue, and does not improve in the morning. His blood pressure is elevated at 162/100 mmHg on admission. Hypertension was previously well-controlled on amlodipine. The isolated unilateral ptosis in the context of ascending limb weakness and global areflexia represents a challenging diagnostic puzzle — the ptosis triggers workup for myasthenia gravis, Horner syndrome, and oculomotor nerve palsy, while the systemic weakness and areflexia remain unexplained by any single cranial nerve etiology. The key insight is that global areflexia is not a feature of myasthenia gravis or Horner syndrome.

Pattern consistent with severe demyelinating polyneuropathy with conduction block. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Guillain-Barré syndrome, severe AIDP with cranial nerve variant (unilateral left ptosis), seronegative for anti-GQ1b

differential.key_features: AChR/MuSK negative; RNS no decrement; SFEMG normal jitter; edrophonium negative; ice pack negative; global areflexia NOT seen in MG
No ophthalmoplegia (full EOM); no ataxia; anti-GQ1b negative; demyelinating NCS (not typical for MFS)
Full extraocular movements — CN III palsy would cause ophthalmoplegia; MRI normal cranial nerves
Partial ptosis pattern atypical for Horner (would expect anhidrosis, miosis); imaging normal — no Horner tract lesion

optimal_actions.action: NCS/EMG with RNS and SFEMG — suspected MG vs GBS
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Severe demyelinating GBS pattern; NMJ testing negative

optimal_actions.action: AChR and MuSK antibodies + ice pack test

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Normal brain/CN III; lumbosacral nerve root enhancement

critical_actions: Recognize that global areflexia is NOT a feature of myasthenia gravis — this clinical finding immediately suggests GBS over MG
Complete NMJ testing (RNS, SFEMG, edrophonium, ice pack, antibodies) to exclude MG before diagnosing GBS with atypical cranial features
Anti-GQ1b negative excludes Miller Fisher syndrome — and MFS would not cause ascending limb weakness anyway
MRI brain to exclude CN III palsy (Horner syndrome, aneurysm) as central cause of unilateral ptosis
IVIG is the correct treatment — GBS does not respond to pyridostigmine (would be inappropriate MG treatment)
contraindicated_actions: Pyridostigmine for presumed MG without confirming NMJ diagnosis
key_reasoning_points: Unilateral ptosis in GBS — rare but documented; represents isolated levator palpebrae cranial nerve involvement within the GBS spectrum
The critical differentiator from MG is GLOBAL AREFLEXIA — myasthenia gravis never causes areflexia; reflexes may be preserved or even brisk
NCS/EMG is the pivotal test — severe demyelinating polyneuropathy is the GBS signature; NMJ testing is normal
Anti-GQ1b antibody syndrome (Miller Fisher) requires ophthalmoplegia + ataxia + areflexia — this patient has ptosis but FULL EOM and NO ataxia
Ice pack test and edrophonium challenge definitively exclude MG when negative

red_herrings.data_point: Left unilateral ptosis as presenting cranial nerve finding
red_herrings.intended_effect: Immediately trigger myasthenia gravis workup and possibly initiate pyridostigmine treatment before GBS is recognized
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Global areflexia on neurological exam is incompatible with MG; the ptosis is a cranial nerve manifestation of GBS; NCS/EMG and CSF confirm the true diagnosis

red_herrings.data_point: No recent illness recalled by patient
red_herrings.intended_effect: Reduce suspicion for post-infectious GBS since no antecedent illness is identified
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: GBS can occur without an identified preceding illness in up to 30% of cases; absent infection history does not exclude GBS — NCS/EMG and CSF are required regardless

metadata.difficulty_description: Unilateral ptosis as GBS cranial nerve manifestation — closely mimics myasthenia gravis; global areflexia is the discriminating finding that refocuses the diagnosis on GBS
